advance_fee_inheritance:
SCAM PATTERN: Advance fee: inheritance, lottery, customs-held goods (id advance_fee_inheritance, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): The victim is told by email, letter, social media or phone that they are owed a large sum (an inheritance from someone with their surname, an overseas lottery win, a rebate, or gold or jewellery held at customs) and must first pay taxes, legal, banking or release fees. Each payment triggers a new fee with an excuse why it cannot come out of the windfall, and fraudsters stress secrecy and urgency.
Channels: email, social, call, sms. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, gift_card, crypto.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented
What the fraudster typically claims: a relative with your surname died and left millions; you have won an international lottery, pay the processing fee; your gold is held at customs, pay clearance to release it; just one more tax payment and the funds will be released; we can't deduct the fee from the inheritance, it must be paid upfront
What victims are coached to say or do: keep this deal secret and do not tell anyone; act quickly before the money goes to the government; think how close you are and how much you have already paid
Red flags: payment of 'fees' or 'taxes' to release an inheritance, prize or parcel; payee overseas or a 'lawyer' or 'agent' account; series of escalating fee payments; customer says they will receive a much larger sum soon; told to keep the windfall secret; no lottery was entered
aeps_biometric_misuse:
SCAM PATTERN: AePS biometric (cloned fingerprint) withdrawal (id aeps_biometric_misuse, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters harvest Aadhaar numbers and fingerprints (for example from property registration documents downloaded from state registration websites, or captured during Aadhaar updates), make silicone or polymer fingerprint clones, and use AePS business-correspondent devices or apps to withdraw money from linked bank accounts without any OTP. Victims often notice only when balances fall, sometimes in accounts they rarely use.
Channels: in_person, app. Payment rails: aeps, cash.
Typical victims: Holders of Aadhaar-linked bank accounts, including property buyers/sellers whose registration documents are online and senior citizens with little-used accounts (Moneylife 2022, 2023).
What the fraudster typically claims: (no caller script; victim reports) money was withdrawn through a bank mitra / customer service point without any OTP; (victim reports) I never used that account but cash was withdrawn with my Aadhaar
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: cash withdrawals via AePS or a business correspondent that you did not make; debits without any OTP or card use; fingerprints captured by an agent during an Aadhaar update or enrolment; property registration documents with your fingerprints are available online; withdrawals from an account you rarely use
ai_voice_clone_emergency:
SCAM PATTERN: AI-cloned voice of a relative asking for urgent money (id ai_voice_clone_emergency, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Scammers collect a short voice sample of a person from social media videos or a 'wrong number' call, clone it with AI, and then call that person's parents, relatives or friends sounding distressed (sobbing, under threat, in hospital) to ask for immediate money. Urgency and emotion are used to stop the victim from checking with the real person, and payment is usually requested via UPI to an unfamiliar account.
Channels: call, whatsapp, video. Payment rails: upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Parents, elderly relatives and acquaintances of people whose voice is available online; reported cases include a Noida mother and a 67-year-old Kolkata man.
What the fraudster typically claims: Mummy, I am in trouble, send money right now; I have been caught, please transfer quickly; a relative is admitted in hospital and needs money urgently; my phone is not working, this is a friend's number
What victims are coached to say or do: pay immediately by UPI without taking time to verify; do not call back on the old number, use this new number
Red flags: voice of a known person calling from an unknown number; sobbing or panicked tone and claim of threat, hospital or arrest; request for immediate UPI payment to an account not in the relative's name; caller resists verification or call-back; odd word choices or form of address unlike the real person
apk_malware_invite:
SCAM PATTERN: Malicious APK on WhatsApp (wedding invite, bank, PM-Kisan, e-challan) (id apk_malware_invite, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Victims receive an .apk file or link on WhatsApp, SMS or Telegram disguised as a wedding invitation, bank KYC/rewards app, PM-Kisan scheme app, RTO e-challan or gas bill update. Installing it gives the malware access to SMS, contacts and banking data; it reads and forwards bank OTPs, overlays fake banking screens and often forwards itself to the victim's contacts, after which money is debited to mule accounts.
Channels: whatsapp, sms, telegram, app. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; wedding-season recipients (Himachal police), PM-Kisan-themed lures suggest farmers and scheme beneficiaries but no profile is stated by sources.
What the fraudster typically claims: you are invited to our wedding, open the card; your traffic challan is pending, download the app to pay; your PM Kisan instalment is pending, install the app; your bank KYC or reward points will expire, update via this app; your gas connection will be cut, update the bill
What victims are coached to say or do: install the update to complete the process
Red flags: a file ending in .apk sent on WhatsApp or Telegram; wedding card, challan, PM-Kisan or bank update sent as an app rather than a PDF or image; message from an unknown number or a contact's hacked account; app asks for SMS, call, contacts, accessibility or VPN permissions; phone overheats, restarts or sends messages to contacts by itself; OTP SMSes you did not see, followed by debits
army_buyer_seller_olx:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake army / CISF buyer or seller on OLX and Facebook Marketplace (id army_buyer_seller_olx, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters pose as Army, CISF or paramilitary personnel on classifieds such as OLX, Quikr and social-media marketplaces. As 'buyers' they agree to the seller's price, claim a remote posting so they can only pay online, send a fake payment screenshot and then QR codes or links that, when the seller enters the UPI PIN, debit the seller repeatedly; as 'sellers' they list cheap vehicles or goods because of a transfer, send fake service ID cards and collect advances and add-on charges without delivering.
Channels: marketplace, whatsapp, call, social. Payment rails: upi, wallet, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: People selling or buying used goods, vehicles and furniture on online classifieds; sources note even service personnel have been debited.
What the fraudster typically claims: I am in the army, I am posted far away so I will pay online; I have paid, see the screenshot; there is a technical issue; scan this QR code to receive your money; outsiders are not allowed in the camp, pay the advance and we will deliver; it was a mistake, scan this one to get the refund
What victims are coached to say or do: scan the QR code and enter your UPI PIN to receive the payment; send a small amount first to verify the account; pay the advance now because you cannot visit the camp
Red flags: buyer or seller says they are in the army/CISF and recently transferred; refuses in-person inspection or meeting, citing camp rules; sends an army ID card or Aadhaar as proof; seller is asked to scan a QR code or enter UPI PIN to 'receive' money; fake payment screenshot followed by 'technical issue'; advance or extra charges demanded before delivery
bank_fraud_dept_impersonation:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake bank fraud team: 'block the unauthorised transaction', share OTP or move money to a safe/RBI account (id bank_fraud_dept_impersonation, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller posing as the bank's fraud, security or card department (sometimes quoting the customer's name or date of birth) says there is an unauthorised transaction or the account will be frozen, and to 'block' or 'reverse' it the customer must share an OTP/PIN/CVV or install a screen-sharing app and type in card details. A related script, seen in digital-arrest cases, asks victims to move funds to an 'RBI' or verification account for safekeeping; RBI holds no accounts for individuals, so such transfers go straight to mule accounts.
Channels: call, sms, whatsapp, app. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: General public; senior citizens are frequently targeted with account-freeze calls (Moneylife, Apr 2026).
What the fraudster typically claims: we have detected an unauthorised transaction on your account; your account will be frozen unless you verify now; share the OTP you just received so we can block the transaction; install this app so our team can secure your account; move your balance to this safe account until the issue is fixed
What victims are coached to say or do: type the card details and OTP into the app yourself instead of reading them out (screen-sharing variant)
Red flags: unsolicited call about an unauthorised transaction or account freeze; caller already knows your name or date of birth to sound genuine; asks for OTP, PIN or CVV to 'block' or 'reverse' a transaction; asks you to install a screen-sharing or support app and type in card details; asks you to transfer money to a 'safe', 'secure' or RBI account; call not from the number printed on your card or the bank's official 1600-series number
bank_safe_account_impersonation:
SCAM PATTERN: Bank/police 'safe account' impersonation (id bank_safe_account_impersonation, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller or texter posing as the victim's bank fraud team (sometimes the police, National Crime Agency or an internet provider) says the account is compromised and the money must be moved immediately to a new 'safe account', which the criminal controls. Calls often use spoofed numbers, real staff names and data from earlier phishing or breaches, and the victim may be told their own bank is under investigation and coached to lie if the real bank asks why they are moving money.
Channels: call, sms, email. Payment rails: bank_transfer, card, cash.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (UK Finance says criminals research victims using breach data; Lloyds and Santander case studies involve older customers)
What the fraudster typically claims: your account has been compromised and money is being taken; move everything to this safe account now or you will lose it; someone at your branch is under investigation, so do not tell them; look up my name on LinkedIn to check I am genuine; if your bank calls, say the payment is genuine
What victims are coached to say or do: tell the bank the payment is genuine if they call; do not tell bank staff the real reason, the bank is under investigation; keep this secret, it is a confidential investigation; give the bank a different reason for moving the money; stay on the line while you make the transfer
Red flags: unexpected call or text saying your account is at risk; instruction to move money to a new or 'safe' account; caller ID shows the bank's real number or a named employee; told your own bank or branch staff are involved in fraud; told to keep the 'investigation' secret or give a false reason for the payment; asked to install remote access software or approve payments
betting_gaming_app:
SCAM PATTERN: Illegal betting / online money gaming app (id betting_gaming_app, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Illegal betting and online money-gaming apps lure users into depositing money into an in-app wallet with fake promises of large returns or winnings. The government says such apps have generated over Rs 400 crore of criminal proceeds (citing the ED), and the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 bans online money gaming along with its promotion, advertising and payments.
Channels: app, social, whatsapp, telegram, web. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer, crypto.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented in sources reviewed.
What the fraudster typically claims: deposit and win double in minutes; guaranteed winning tips, join our Telegram; add more to your wallet to unlock withdrawal; everyone is winning, do not miss today's match
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: app installed from a link or APK, not an official store; deposit money into a game wallet to bet or 'predict'; each deposit goes to a different personal UPI ID or account; promises of doubling money or guaranteed winnings; withdrawal delayed, blocked or needing a further deposit; promoted by influencers or Telegram 'tipsters'
bitcoin_atm_cash_to_crypto:
SCAM PATTERN: Bitcoin/crypto ATM cash deposit ('safety locker') (id bitcoin_atm_cash_to_crypto, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): Usually the cash-out stage of a government, business (bank, Amazon) or tech-support impersonation scam: the victim is told their money is at risk or tied to a crime and must be 'protected' or a problem fixed. They are instructed to withdraw cash from their bank, go to a specific Bitcoin ATM (sometimes described as a 'safety locker') and scan a QR code sent by text, which sends the cash irreversibly to the scammer's crypto wallet, often while kept on the phone.
Channels: call, sms, web, in_person. Payment rails: cash, crypto.
Typical victims: Older adults: FTC (1H 2024) says people 60+ were over three times as likely to report a Bitcoin ATM loss and accounted for about 71% of losses; IC3 2025 says 60+ lost $257.5m of the $389m reported at crypto ATMs/kiosks.
What the fraudster typically claims: your bank account has been hacked, move your cash to a safe place; deposit the cash in this Bitcoin machine to protect it; scan the QR code I just texted you; this is a government safety locker; stay on the line until the deposit is done
What victims are coached to say or do: withdraw the cash and go to this specific Bitcoin ATM; scan the QR code we text you; stay on the phone while you do it
Red flags: large cash withdrawal by an older customer with no clear purpose; customer on the phone during the withdrawal; mention of a Bitcoin ATM, crypto kiosk or QR code; story about protecting money, a hacked account or a government investigation; repeat withdrawals over consecutive days; customer asks how much cash can be taken out today
boss_impersonation_whatsapp:
SCAM PATTERN: Boss / CEO / senior officer impersonation on WhatsApp (id boss_impersonation_whatsapp, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters message employees or subordinates from a new number using the boss's photo as display picture, or from the boss's genuine WhatsApp account after hijacking it (I4C's 2026 'Boss Scam': malicious 'Statement of Account'/RBI/MCA zip files take over WhatsApp Web), or save their own number under 'CEO' on a compromised phone. Claiming to be busy, travelling or in a meeting, they instruct urgent fund transfers to mule accounts or the purchase of gift cards (e.g. Amazon) whose codes must be sent back, citing client gifts, staff incentives or confidential deals.
Channels: whatsapp, email, sms. Payment rails: neft_rtgs, imps, upi, bank_transfer, gift_card.
Typical victims: Finance and accounts staff, CFOs, Chartered Accountants and company directors (per I4C), and subordinates of senior officers or executives.
What the fraudster typically claims: I am in a meeting, process this payment immediately; buy Amazon gift cards for clients and send me the codes; I am travelling and unreachable, handle this urgently; use this new account for the vendor; forward this statement file to the finance manager for verification
What victims are coached to say or do: I am busy in a meeting, do not call, just process it; I am travelling and unreachable, handle it urgently; send the gift card codes back to me on chat
Red flags: urgent payment or gift-card request from the 'boss' over WhatsApp or email only; new number with the boss's photo, or 'CEO' contact that changed recently; sender says they are in a meeting or travelling and cannot take calls; payee is a new beneficiary or individual account; request to send gift card codes as photos; request arrives right after a zip file was opened on a work computer
call_merging_otp:
SCAM PATTERN: Call-merging OTP theft (id call_merging_otp, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller posing as an event organiser or job interviewer says a mutual friend gave them the victim's number and asks the victim to merge in a call from the 'friend'. The second call is actually the bank's genuine OTP verification call triggered by the fraudster, so the fraudster hears the OTP and completes a transaction or account takeover.
Channels: call. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented
What the fraudster typically claims: your friend gave me your number; my friend is calling from another number, please merge the call; I am calling about the event invitation; this is regarding your job interview
What victims are coached to say or do: merge the incoming call with this one so we can all talk
Red flags: unknown caller says a friend gave them your number; caller asks you to merge or conference in another incoming call; an automated bank call or OTP call arrives during the conversation; you receive an OTP for a transaction you did not start; caller pretends to invite you to an event or a job interview
ceo_fraud:
SCAM PATTERN: CEO / boss impersonation (urgent payment or gift cards) (id ceo_fraud, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A fraudster impersonates the CEO, a senior executive or the victim's supervisor, usually by compromising or spoofing their email, and tells a finance team member to make an urgent payment to a new account or change payment details. A common variant asks an employee to move to WhatsApp and buy gift cards (e.g. for staff incentives or client gifts), then send the redemption codes.
Channels: email, whatsapp, call, video. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, gift_card.
Typical victims: Mostly businesses, especially staff responsible for making payments (UK Finance; SPF). Low volume but high value: UK Finance says CEO fraud has the highest average loss of the eight APP types (just over £28,000 per case in 2025).
What the fraudster typically claims: I need you to make an urgent payment today, I'm in a meeting; can you send me your mobile number, let's continue on WhatsApp; buy some gift cards for client gifts and send me the codes; please process this to the new account before cut-off
What victims are coached to say or do: continue the conversation on your personal WhatsApp; buy the gift cards in person, scratch them and send me the redemption codes
Red flags: urgent payment request from a senior executive by email or chat; instruction to bypass normal approval or keep it confidential; request to switch to a personal WhatsApp number; request to buy gift cards for 'staff incentives' or 'client gifts'; new payee account for a request supposedly from the boss; sender address or display name slightly off
courier_fraud_cash_collection:
SCAM PATTERN: Courier fraud (fake police/bank sends a courier for cash, cards or gold) (id courier_fraud_cash_collection, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller posing as a police officer or bank employee claims a card has been used fraudulently or that bank staff or a jeweller are corrupt, and enlists the victim in an 'investigation'. The victim is told to withdraw cash, buy gold, jewellery or watches, or hand over their card and PIN, which a courier then collects from their home; contact can continue for days or weeks with repeat collections.
Channels: call, whatsapp, in_person. Payment rails: cash, card.
Typical victims: Older people: City of London Police say those aged 70+ are the majority of victims and 76-96 year olds about 62% of reports; London and surrounding counties about 65% of victims (2025). In Singapore GOIS cash/gold handovers, 40.8% of victims were 65+ (1H 2026).
What the fraudster typically claims: we have arrested someone using your card; staff at your branch are taking money from accounts and we need evidence; withdraw the cash so we can check it for fingerprints, it will be returned; a courier will collect your card so you do not have to come in; buy gold from this jeweller to help our undercover operation
What victims are coached to say or do: do not discuss this with anyone, including your bank; lie to the bank about why you are withdrawing the money; ignore or get around the bank's security checks; do not contact your bank as it could cause issues with the investigation; write your PIN down and put it in a separate envelope for the courier
Red flags: large or repeated cash withdrawals by an older customer; unusual purchases of gold, jewellery or luxury watches; customer says police or bank asked for help with an investigation; courier or taxi arranged to collect cash, card or PIN from home; customer told not to speak to branch staff or family; caller asked customer to read or key in their PIN
courier_parcel:
SCAM PATTERN: Courier or parcel case (id courier_parcel, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller claiming to be from a courier company or customs says a parcel in the victim's name holds drugs, passports or contraband, then 'transfers' the call to fake police who demand money to settle the case. Often turns into a digital arrest.
Channels: call, video, sms, whatsapp, web. Payment rails: neft_rtgs, imps, upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: General public; documented cases include salaried professionals such as software engineers in Bengaluru (TNM 2024).
What the fraudster typically claims: A parcel booked with your Aadhaar contains drugs and fake passports.; Press 1 to speak to the courier officer; we are connecting you to the police.; a parcel in your name with drugs and passports was seized at Mumbai airport; your Aadhaar was used to send this parcel to Taiwan; I am transferring your call to Mumbai police/customs; transfer the amount for RBI verification; it will be refunded in 30 days
What victims are coached to say or do: take the calls from an isolated room with your camera on; transfer money to the 'RBI' account for verification; it will be returned within 30 days
Red flags: A parcel the victim never sent; Call 'transferred' to police or narcotics; Demand for a fee, fine or verification deposit; automated or live call about a parcel you never sent; parcel 'seized' at airport with drugs, passports or contraband; call transferred to customs, narcotics or Mumbai police
credit_card_limit_or_fee:
SCAM PATTERN: Credit card limit increase / annual fee waiver / activation / new card offer (id credit_card_limit_or_fee, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Callers or messages posing as the card issuer or an NBFC offer a credit limit enhancement, annual-fee waiver, card activation help or a new premium/lifetime-free card, and ask the customer to call a mobile number, fill a 'form', open a link or install an app, then share OTP/PIN or approve a token Re 1 payment. The captured details or malicious APK are used for unauthorised card and account transactions.
Channels: call, sms, whatsapp, social, app, web. Payment rails: card, upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Credit card holders and applicants; documented cases include a businessman in Andheri (Moneylife 2022) and a frequent flyer lured by a Facebook lounge-access card ad (Moneylife 2025).
What the fraudster typically claims: you are eligible for a credit limit increase today; we will waive your annual fee if you verify now; your new card needs activation; share the OTP; fill this form to get a lifetime-free card with lounge access; pay Re 1 to confirm your card upgrade
What victims are coached to say or do: fill in the 'form' (actually an APK) sent on WhatsApp while the caller waits
Red flags: unsolicited offer to raise your credit limit or waive the annual fee; caller asks you to fill a form sent on WhatsApp or install an app/APK; asked to share OTP, CVV or approve a Re 1 payment to 'verify'; contact number is a mobile number, not the issuer's official line; card offer seen in a social media ad followed by a call
credit_card_reward_points:
SCAM PATTERN: Credit card reward points redemption / expiry lure (id credit_card_reward_points, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Messages or calls in a card issuer's name offer to redeem or 'save' expiring reward points or cashback through a link, form or app; the link or APK captures card number, CVV, OTPs and SMS, and fraudsters then make card or e-commerce transactions. Note: the sources reachable in this run document these mechanics under card-offer, cashback and bank-SMS APK pretexts; no fetched source described the reward-points wording specifically.
Channels: sms, whatsapp, call, app, web, social. Payment rails: card, gift_card, upi.
Typical victims: Credit card holders; no specific profile documented in cited sources.
What the fraudster typically claims: your reward points worth a large amount expire today; redeem now; download this app to convert your points to cash; fill this form to claim your card benefit; share the OTP to credit the points to your account
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: message saying reward points or cashback will expire today; link or APK to 'redeem' points or claim an offer; form asking for card number, expiry, CVV or OTP; sender is a mobile number or unofficial WhatsApp account; OTPs arriving for purchases you did not make
crypto_investment:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake crypto / forex platform and 'pig butchering' (id crypto_investment, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters build trust over days or weeks through chats, social media or task groups, then persuade the victim to invest in cryptocurrency, forex or another 'lucrative scheme' on a fake app or website guided by 'teachers' or mentors. The platform shows rising balances, but withdrawals are blocked and more payments are demanded until the victim stops; the government links such 'pig butchering' operations to scam compounds abroad.
Channels: whatsapp, telegram, social, app, web. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer, crypto.
Typical victims: Unemployed youth, students, housewives and needy people (government alert summarised by CRPF Cyber Byte, March 2025, citing the MHA annual report).
What the fraudster typically claims: I made big profits trading crypto, let me teach you; this platform gives guaranteed daily returns; follow the teacher's signals in the group; your account needs a deposit before you can withdraw
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: online contact who builds a friendship before talking about investing; crypto, bitcoin or forex trading on an app or site shared by link; a 'teacher', mentor or group admin guides each trade; balance grows quickly but withdrawal is blocked; asked to pay more to unlock, upgrade or verify the account; payments go to individual bank accounts or UPI IDs rather than a registered exchange
delivery_toll_smishing:
SCAM PATTERN: Parcel redelivery / unpaid toll text (smishing) (id delivery_toll_smishing, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A text, iMessage or email posing as a postal or courier company (the FTC cites USPS, UPS and FedEx; UK texts use brands such as Royal Mail or Evri) or a toll agency says a parcel could not be delivered or a toll is unpaid and asks for a small fee via a link. The fake site harvests card details, online banking credentials and one-time passcodes; criminals then add the card to Apple Pay or Google Pay, log in from a new device, or follow up with a fake bank 'fraud team' call that leads into a safe account scam.
Channels: sms, email, web. Payment rails: card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; SPF (1H 2026) says phishing victims were mostly aged 30-49 (40.8%)
What the fraudster typically claims: your parcel could not be delivered due to an invalid address; pay a small redelivery fee to reschedule; you have an outstanding toll balance, pay now to avoid penalties; enter the code we sent to confirm your payment
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: text about a failed delivery or unpaid toll with a link; small redelivery or toll fee requested; sender is a random email address or overseas number; OTP or token approval requested right after entering card details; new device or digital wallet added to the card shortly after; follow-up call from 'the bank' about suspicious activity
digital_arrest:
SCAM PATTERN: Digital arrest (id digital_arrest, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Callers pose as police, CBI, ED, narcotics, customs or court officials, claim the victim is linked to a crime, keep them on a video call for hours and demand money to 'clear their name' or for 'verification'.
Channels: call, video, whatsapp, sms. Payment rails: neft_rtgs, imps, upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: People of every class and age group (PM, Mann Ki Baat 2024); senior citizens are repeatedly named among victims by the Supreme Court and in bank-intervention cases.
What the fraudster typically claims: Your Aadhaar or phone number has been used in money laundering or drug trafficking.; You are under digital arrest and cannot leave the call.; Transfer your savings to an RBI or court account for verification; it will be returned.; your parcel contains drugs and fake passports and has been seized; a money-laundering case is registered against your Aadhaar; you are under digital arrest until the investigation is complete
What victims are coached to say or do: stay on the video call and do not disconnect; isolate yourself and do not tell anyone, including family; keep the matter confidential because it is a secret investigation; move your money to the given account for verification; it will be refunded; give the bank a personal reason (e.g. buying property) when breaking FDs (observed: victim gave this reason while fraudsters stayed on the phone)
Red flags: A video or phone call from someone in uniform or claiming to be an officer; Told they are under 'digital arrest' and must stay on camera; Threat of arrest, a case, or frozen accounts; Told to keep it secret from family; Asked to move money to a 'safe' or 'verification' account; unsolicited call or video call from someone claiming to be police/CBI/ED/narcotics/RBI
e_challan_apk:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake traffic e-challan / RTO / Parivahan link or APK (id e_challan_apk, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): SMS or WhatsApp messages carrying realistic traffic-violation details claim an e-challan is pending and send a link to a cloned Parivahan/MVD portal or an APK named like 'RTO Challan' or 'e Challan App'. The fake site collects card/UPI details for the 'fine', while the APK grabs SMS and OTPs, takes over WhatsApp, forwards itself to contacts, and is used to drain bank or e-commerce accounts.
Channels: sms, whatsapp, app, web. Payment rails: card, upi, gift_card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Vehicle owners; general public. CloudSEK found Gujarat and Karnataka most affected (IANS 2024).
What the fraudster typically claims: your vehicle has a pending traffic e-challan; pay your fine today to avoid court action; download the RTO challan app to see the violation; your challan details are attached; click to view; pay the challan online through this link
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: challan message from a private mobile number or WhatsApp; link that is not echallan.parivahan.gov.in or the state MVD site; asked to download an APK file to view or pay the challan; site asks for vehicle number then shows a fake security check; new app asks for SMS, contacts and default-messaging permissions
electricity_disconnection:
SCAM PATTERN: Electricity disconnection threat (id electricity_disconnection, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): An SMS or call says power will be cut tonight because a bill is unpaid, and gives a personal number to call; the 'officer' then asks for a payment or an app install.
Channels: sms, whatsapp, call, app. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: General public; documented victims include senior citizens and retirees (Tribune, Jalandhar 2022).
What the fraudster typically claims: Your electricity will be disconnected at 9:30 pm. Call the officer immediately.; your electricity will be disconnected tonight at 9:30 pm; your previous month's bill was not updated; call the electricity officer immediately on this number; pay rs 10 / rs 100 to update your previous entry; download this app so I can update your bill
What victims are coached to say or do: install the remote support app the 'officer' names and keep the call going while making the small payment
Red flags: SMS from a personal mobile number; Disconnection 'tonight'; Pay to an individual or through a link; message from a 10-digit mobile number, not the discom's sender ID; threat that power will be cut tonight at a specific time; asked to call an 'electricity officer' on a personal number
epfo_pf_withdrawal:
SCAM PATTERN: EPFO / PF withdrawal or claim 'processing fee' (id epfo_pf_withdrawal, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): People seeking PF withdrawals, transfers, KYC corrections or claim settlement are approached by 'agents', cyber-cafe operators, fintech intermediaries or look-alike EPFO/labour-ministry portals that charge fees for services EPFO provides free, or collect UAN, Aadhaar, bank and OTP details. EPFO warns this exposes members' financial data; RBI also documents fake helpline numbers planted in search results that ask callers for card or account details.
Channels: call, web, whatsapp, in_person, social. Payment rails: upi, bank_transfer, cash.
Typical victims: EPFO members, employers and pensioners (EPFO press release, Jun 2025); no further profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: your PF claim is stuck; pay a processing fee to release it; I can get your PF withdrawn today for a charge; share the OTP to update your KYC on the EPFO portal; register on this portal for the government employment scheme
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: someone offers to speed up a PF claim or withdrawal for a fee; request for UAN password, Aadhaar OTP or bank details by phone or WhatsApp; EPFO 'helpline' number found via search engine or social media; website or app that is not epfindia.gov.in / UMANG claiming to be EPFO or a labour-ministry scheme; demand to pay before the claim is released
fake_charity_disaster:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake donation drive (temple, disaster relief, needy person) (id fake_charity_disaster, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): During disasters (floods, landslides), major religious events (e.g. the Ayodhya Ram temple consecration) or via hijacked friends' social-media accounts, fraudsters circulate appeals with QR codes, UPI IDs or bank accounts that imitate official relief funds or temple trusts, or ask for help for a 'needy person'. Look-alike UPI IDs that differ by one letter from an official fund, and QR codes sent privately on WhatsApp, route the donation to the fraudster.
Channels: social, whatsapp, sms, call, web. Payment rails: upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (devotees and well-wishers responding to disasters or religious events).
What the fraudster typically claims: donate for the Ram temple construction, scan this QR code; contribute to flood relief through this UPI ID; give your WhatsApp number and I will send the donation QR; help this needy family urgently; the trust is collecting donations through this account
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: donation QR code or UPI ID received on WhatsApp or social media rather than an official portal; UPI ID or payee name slightly different from the official relief fund or trust; caller or page asks for your WhatsApp number to send a QR code; appeal timed to a disaster or big religious event; request for money for a 'needy person' from a friend's account
fake_cybercrime_legal_notice:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake police / I4C / CBI legal notice email (id fake_cybercrime_legal_notice, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Emails with PDF 'notices' bearing logos of CBI, IB, I4C or a Commissioner of Police and fake 'top secret' stamps accuse recipients of visiting illegal sites or offences involving minors and demand a reply within 24-48 hours to avoid arrest or court action. They are sent in bulk from non-government domains; replying opens the door to extortion or a digital-arrest style follow-up.
Channels: email. Payment rails: upi.
Typical victims: Random recipients from email lists; documented recipients include a student (Moneylife 2024).
What the fraudster typically claims: a court order has been issued against you for visiting illegal websites; respond within 48 hours or face serious legal action; this is an official warning from the Commissioner of Police; reply to this official court order warning
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: email or PDF notice citing a court order for viewing illegal content; logos of several agencies and 'certified'/'top secret' stamps; deadline of 24-48 hours to respond; sender domain is not a government (.gov.in/.nic.in) address; poor translation or emojis in the subject line
fake_ecommerce_site:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake shopping / sale website or social-media shop (id fake_ecommerce_site, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters build look-alike websites of known brands, restaurants or new 'stores' and promote them through social-media and search ads with very deep discounts on phones, electronics, shoes or food. The buyer pays online (UPI, card or transfer) but nothing is delivered, a used or different item arrives, or card details are harvested; some sites promise a free gift and then a fake customer-service caller demands refundable handling or GST fees. Sites change their URLs when reported.
Channels: web, social, app, call. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer, wallet.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (online shoppers attracted by deep discounts).
What the fraudster typically claims: mega sale: iPhone at 80% off, today only; limited stock, pay now to confirm the order; free gift with your order, pay the refundable handling charge; cash on delivery not available for this offer; your order is on hold until you pay GST
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: price far below the market for a high-value item; site reached through a social-media or search ad, recently created domain or misspelled brand name; only prepaid payment, no cash on delivery, or payment to a personal UPI ID; no reviews or many non-delivery complaints; 'customer care' calls asking for extra handling, GST or gift-release fees
fake_friend_call_sg:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake friend call ('guess who') loan request (id fake_friend_call_sg, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller from an unknown number (phone or WhatsApp) asks the victim to guess who is calling, poses as an acquaintance, and says they lost their phone and changed number. After establishing rapport, the 'friend' asks for an urgent loan, for example to pay renovation contractors, new-business costs or suppliers, which the victim sends by PayNow to a bank account belonging to an unknown person; some callers also push links or app installs.
Channels: call, whatsapp, sms. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wallet.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented on the ScamShield page
What the fraudster typically claims: guess who this is; I lost my phone, this is my new number; I need to pay my renovation contractor, can you lend me some money; I'm opening a new business and need to pay a vendor; click this link / install this app to help me
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: call from an unknown number that starts with 'guess who I am'; friend claims a lost phone and new number; urgent loan request for renovation, business opening or supplier payment; payee is a third party, not the friend; request to click a link or install an app
fake_job_offer_fee:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake job offer with fees (incl. overseas 'cyber slavery' recruitment) (id fake_job_offer_fee, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters harvest job-seeker details from job portals or advertise government, airline, IT or overseas jobs, hold fake interviews and send fake offer or selection letters, then collect staged fees for registration, insurance, security deposit, training or visa processing until the victim stops paying. An overseas variant uses fake job offers from dubious firms and unscrupulous agents to send Indians to scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, where they are forced into cyber fraud ('cyber slavery').
Channels: whatsapp, email, call, web, social. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Job seekers, including highly educated engineers, MBA, MCA and pharma graduates (Hyderabad police, 2025); unemployed youth and students lured abroad (CRPF Cyber Byte citing MHA, 2025).
What the fraudster typically claims: you are selected, pay the registration fee to receive your offer letter; pay a refundable security deposit to confirm your joining; training and uniform charges are required before joining; well-paid job abroad, the agent will arrange travel; your visa and job abroad are approved, pay the processing fee
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: offer arrives without a proper application or after a very short interview; payment demanded for registration, insurance, security deposit, training, uniform or offer letter; each payment is followed by a new fee or a 'payment gateway stuck' excuse; offer letter or appointment from a government body or airline sent on WhatsApp or Gmail; overseas job through a private agent, especially to Cambodia, Laos or Myanmar; fees go to personal bank accounts or UPI IDs
fake_payment_screenshot:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake UPI payment screenshot / spoof payment app (id fake_payment_screenshot, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A buyer shows a shopkeeper or online seller a doctored payment screenshot or a spoof payment-app screen as 'proof' that money was sent, takes the goods, and leaves; no money reaches the account. In marketplace scams the fake screenshot is the opening move before the fraudster sends QR codes that debit the seller.
Channels: in_person, marketplace, whatsapp. Payment rails: upi.
Typical victims: Shopkeepers and small merchants (Moneylife, 2026) and online classified sellers (Delhi Police).
What the fraudster typically claims: payment done, see the screenshot; there was a technical issue, the money will come; I have paid, check your phone later
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: customer shows a screenshot or their own phone screen instead of you receiving a credit alert; no sound-box or bank credit notification for the payment; customer is in a hurry and leaves quickly; buyer says payment is done but asks you to scan a QR to 'receive' it
fake_support_refund:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake customer care number (id fake_support_refund, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A 'customer care' number found online, or a caller offering a refund, asks the victim to approve a UPI request, enter their PIN or install a screen-sharing app so the 'refund' can be processed.
Channels: call, web, social, sms, app. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: People seeking help with a failed transaction, refund, booking or service complaint; RBI notes those new to digital payments are especially at risk.
What the fraudster typically claims: Enter your PIN to receive the refund.; Install this app so I can help you.; I am calling from customer care about your complaint; to process your refund, fill this complaint form with your card details; enter your UPI PIN to receive the refund; install this app so I can help you get your money back
What victims are coached to say or do: enter your UPI PIN to receive the refund (receiving money never needs a PIN); type your card details into the complaint portal while on the call
Red flags: Helpline number found through a search result or social media; Asked to enter UPI PIN or approve a request to 'receive' money; Asked to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or a support app; helpline number found via search engine, maps or social media; 'customer care' number is a 10-digit mobile number; call arrives right after you complained publicly on social media
foreign_gift_customs:
SCAM PATTERN: Gift from foreign friend stuck at customs (id foreign_gift_customs, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A new Facebook/Instagram friend or online partner claiming to live in the UK or another foreign country promises to send expensive gifts, jewellery or foreign currency. A caller posing as a customs officer (or 'diplomatic agent') at Mumbai or Delhi airport then says the parcel is held and demands customs duty, clearance or penalty fees into a bank or UPI account, escalating with new charges and threats of legal action until the victim stops paying.
Channels: social, whatsapp, call, sms, email. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Sources describe mainly women (often homemakers) befriended on Facebook, and people on matrimonial sites; men befriended by 'foreign women' have also been targeted.
What the fraudster typically claims: I have sent you a gift with jewellery, a phone and pounds; this is Mumbai airport customs, your parcel is held, pay the duty; the parcel contains foreign currency, you must pay a penalty; pay the clearance fee or you will face legal action; the gift is worth lakhs, the fee is small
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: foreign online friend promises costly gifts or cash; call from a 'customs officer' at an airport about a parcel; duty or clearance fee to be paid into a personal bank account or UPI ID; fees keep rising (currency found, penalty, anti-money laundering); threat of arrest or legal action if fees not paid; photos/videos of the gift sent on WhatsApp
foreign_official_impersonation_sg:
SCAM PATTERN: Government officials impersonation scam (Singapore GOIS, incl. foreign police) (id foreign_official_impersonation_sg, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A call that starts as a bank, telco or financial-institution representative (e.g. about a suspicious card transaction, new phone line or unpaid bill) is 'transferred' to someone posing as an SPF, MAS or MinLaw officer, or in a smaller variant an ICA officer, airline or telco then foreign law enforcement, who accuses the victim of money laundering or other crimes. Victims are told to move money to a government 'safety account', make ATM cash deposits, hand cash, gold or luxury watches to 'officers', or show ID and bank cards on WhatsApp video, sometimes for 'investigation or bail'.
Channels: call, whatsapp, video, in_person. Payment rails: bank_transfer, cash, card.
Typical victims: Mostly older people: SPF says 40.8% of GOIS victims in 1H 2026 were aged 65 and above; phone calls and WhatsApp were the main channels.
What the fraudster typically claims: there is a suspicious transaction on your credit card, let me transfer you to the police; your identity was used for money laundering; transfer your savings to this safety account while we investigate; hand the cash and gold to our officer for investigation; you need to pay bail or a guarantee to the foreign police
What victims are coached to say or do: transfer your money to the government-designated safety account; hand over cash, gold or valuables to the officer who will meet you; show your identity card and bank cards on the video call; deposit the cash at an ATM into the account we give you
Red flags: customer says police, MAS or MinLaw are investigating them; call began as a bank or telco query and was transferred to an 'officer'; transfer to a new account described as a government or safety account; large ATM cash deposits or cash/gold/watch purchases; customer on a WhatsApp video call with an 'officer'; mention of money laundering, bail or foreign police
franchise_dealership:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake franchise / dealership / distributorship offer (id franchise_dealership, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters set up websites or social-media pages that copy a well-known brand (for example a dairy cooperative, fuel company or consumer brand) or a government-style portal and invite people to apply for a franchise, dealership or distributorship. Applicants are then asked to pay registration, application, security deposit, documentation or 'tax' fees in stages into bank accounts, after which the fraudsters vanish. A related I4C-documented variant is a 'foreign investor' offering a business partnership who first needs deposits for documentation and customs.
Channels: web, social, email, call, whatsapp. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (aspiring business owners responding to online ads).
What the fraudster typically claims: your application for the dealership is approved, pay the registration fee; pay the security deposit to confirm your location; limited franchises available in your district; pay documentation and tax charges before the agreement is issued; I am an investor abroad looking for a trusted business partner in India
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: franchise or dealership offer found via an ad, social media or a look-alike website rather than the brand's official site; registration, approval or security-deposit fee demanded upfront to a bank account or UPI ID; pressure to pay quickly to 'reserve' a location; use of brand logos or government emblems as proof; payee name is an individual or unrelated company
gift_card_payment_demand:
SCAM PATTERN: Gift card payment demand (id gift_card_payment_demand, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): Across many storylines (government agency, tech support, family emergency, prize, utility shut-off, romance, or a 'boss' needing gifts for clients), the scammer insists the victim pays by buying gift cards such as Google Play, Apple, Amazon or Razer Gold and reading out or photographing the card numbers and PINs. Victims are kept on the phone and told to spread purchases across several stores so staff do not get suspicious.
Channels: call, email, sms, whatsapp, in_person. Payment rails: gift_card, card, cash.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented
What the fraudster typically claims: pay your fine with Google Play cards to avoid arrest; buy Apple gift cards and read me the numbers; scratch the back and send me a photo of the code; buy them at different shops so it doesn't look odd; I need gift cards for client gifts, I'll reimburse you
What victims are coached to say or do: buy the cards at several different stores so the cashier does not get suspicious; stay on the phone while you buy and load the cards; send the card number and PIN or a photo of the back
Red flags: large or repeated gift card purchases, often at several stores; customer on the phone while buying cards; request to photograph or read out card numbers and PINs; story of paying a government fee, utility bill, tech fix or boss's request with gift cards; cash withdrawal immediately followed by gift card purchases
government_imposter_tax:
SCAM PATTERN: Tax/benefits authority impersonation (HMRC, IRS, SSA, ATO) (id government_imposter_tax, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller, text or email claims to be from the tax or benefits authority (HMRC, IRS, Social Security Administration, ATO) and says the victim owes tax, has a suspended Social Security number or faces arrest, deportation or prosecution unless they pay immediately. A refund variant lures victims to phishing pages. Payment is demanded by bank transfer, gift cards, wire, crypto or payment app, and victims are often told not to tell their bank the real reason.
Channels: call, sms, email, social. Payment rails: bank_transfer, gift_card, wire, crypto, cash.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (one ombudsman case involved a 63-year-old who had recently stopped working)
What the fraudster typically claims: you owe unpaid tax from an audit and must pay today; a warrant has been issued and police will come to your house; your Social Security number has been suspended; you are due a tax refund, click to claim; you must declare your crypto holdings immediately
What victims are coached to say or do: tell the bank the money is for a holiday on a prepaid travel card; do not tell the bank you owe tax or it will close your account; stay on the phone while you are in the branch; keep quiet and do not interrupt while the caller reads out the charges
Red flags: threat of arrest, prison, deportation or licence loss over tax; demand to pay the same day; caller ID matches the agency's real number; payment to a personal account, gift cards, crypto or payment app; told not to tell the bank the payment is for tax; unsolicited text or email about a tax refund with a link
govt_scheme_subsidy:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake government scheme / subsidy registration fee (id govt_scheme_subsidy, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters advertise or message about government schemes (e.g. PM-KUSUM solar pumps, free laptops, free solar flour mills, government loans) through look-alike websites, WhatsApp forwards and calls, then collect Aadhaar, bank details and an upfront 'registration', 'processing' or 'legal insurance' fee, sometimes promising it is refundable. Some variants push links or apps that harvest data; the benefit never arrives.
Channels: whatsapp, sms, call, web, social. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Farmers (PM-KUSUM solar pump fraud), rural women (solar flour mill offer), students (laptop scheme) and loan seekers, per Moneylife reports of PIB/ministry warnings.
What the fraudster typically claims: you are eligible for a solar pump under PM-KUSUM; pay the registration amount; register now for the free laptop scheme; your government loan of Rs 3 lakh is approved; pay the legal insurance charge; the registration fee is refundable after installation; limited seats, apply today
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: scheme promoted via WhatsApp forward or a non-.gov.in website; upfront registration, processing or insurance fee to receive a subsidy or benefit; promise that the fee will be refunded; request for Aadhaar, bank details or OTP to 'register'; forged approval letter on government letterhead
hacked_account_friend_request:
SCAM PATTERN: Hacked or cloned friend's account asking for urgent money (id hacked_account_friend_request, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters take over a person's WhatsApp account (by tricking them into sharing the activation OTP or merging a verification call) or hijack/clone their Facebook or Instagram profile, sometimes using a senior officer's photo as display picture. They then message the victim's contacts and groups saying they are in hospital, stuck in an emergency or need urgent payment, promising to repay in a day or two, and ask for money to a UPI ID or bank account that is not the friend's.
Channels: whatsapp, social, sms. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Friends, relatives and colleagues of the person whose account was hijacked or cloned; general public.
What the fraudster typically claims: I am hospitalised, please transfer money urgently; I am in a meeting, can't talk, please send to this account; my old number has a problem, this is my new number; I will return it tomorrow; send to my friend's UPI, my GPay is not working
What victims are coached to say or do: don't call me, I am in a meeting; just send to this account; send it to this other person's UPI ID, mine is not working; I will repay you in a day or two; I sent you an OTP by mistake, please forward it to me
Red flags: money request by chat from a known contact with no call; new number or duplicate profile of an existing friend; claims to be unable to talk (in a meeting, phone problem, hospital); asks to pay a third party's UPI ID or account; promise to repay within a day or two; message tone, spelling or language unlike the real person
hi_mum_family_text:
SCAM PATTERN: 'Hi Mum' / family member new-number message (id hi_mum_family_text, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A message, usually on WhatsApp or SMS, from an unknown number claims to be the victim's child, parent or friend who has lost or broken their phone. After some chat, the impersonator asks for an urgent payment for a bill, contractor or new phone because they 'cannot access online banking', often to an account in another name, and may ask for further transfers. Phone-call variants use fake lawyers or police, or AI-cloned voices, and ask the victim to keep it secret.
Channels: whatsapp, sms, call, social. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, gift_card, crypto, wallet.
Typical victims: Scamwatch (2022): 82% of Australian family impersonation reports were from people over 55, accounting for 95% of losses, and over two-thirds from women over 55. SPF (1H 2026): social media impersonation victims mostly aged 50-64 (35.5%).
What the fraudster typically claims: hi mum, this is my new number, my phone broke; can you pay this bill for me, my banking app is locked on the new phone; I'll pay you back tomorrow; it's urgent, it has to go today; please don't tell dad
What victims are coached to say or do: keep it secret, do not tell anyone else in the family; pay it to my friend's account because mine is locked
Red flags: message from an unknown number claiming to be a child or relative; story of a lost, broken or new phone; urgent request to pay a bill or invoice for them; payee name does not match the family member; reluctance to take a voice call; request to keep it between you
income_tax_refund:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake income tax refund / tax notice / penalty (id income_tax_refund, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Emails, SMS, WhatsApp messages or calls posing as the Income Tax Department claim a refund is approved (e.g. a Rs 60,000 refund needing 'manual verification'), or that a demand, penalty or prosecution notice is pending with a short deadline, and send a link or file. The link leads to a cloned portal that captures PAN, net-banking passwords, card data and OTPs, or delivers OTP-stealing malware; the department says its communications never contain hyperlinks.
Channels: email, sms, call, web, whatsapp. Payment rails: card, upi, bank_transfer, imps.
Typical victims: Taxpayers; general public. No specific profile documented in cited sources.
What the fraudster typically claims: you are eligible for a refund of Rs 60,000; verify manually through this link; Income Tax Department | Important Message: view message on e-filing portal; a tax demand is outstanding for AY 2025-26; submit documents within 72 hours or face prosecution; download your instant e-PAN card; your tax payment is frozen; pay the challan through this link
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: email or SMS about a tax refund or notice that contains a link; refund 'approved' but you must verify or update bank/card details; sender address or domain that is not incometax.gov.in; request for net-banking password, card number or OTP to receive a refund; threat of penalty or legal action unless paid immediately
insurance_policy_bonus:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake insurance bonus / maturity / lapsed-policy revival (IRDAI/LIC/RBI impersonation) (id insurance_policy_bonus, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Callers posing as insurance company staff, IRDAI or even RBI officials tell policyholders that a policy has matured or earned a large bonus, refund or revival benefit, then demand 'processing fees', charges or taxes before release and keep escalating demands. Variants use fake IRDAI complaint/grievance websites that collect policy, bank and OTP details or payments, and fake insurance call centres selling discounted renewals.
Channels: call, web, sms, email, whatsapp. Payment rails: bank_transfer, neft_rtgs, imps, upi.
Typical victims: Policyholders, including elderly retirees (e.g. an 82-year-old retired professor in Delhi, Moneylife 2022).
What the fraudster typically claims: your policies have matured and you are eligible for a Rs 90 lakh bonus; pay a processing fee to release your bonus; your lapsed policy can be revived with full benefits if you pay now; register your complaint here to get your refund; I am a senior official from RBI handling your insurance payout
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: unsolicited call about a large policy bonus, maturity amount or refund; caller claims to be from IRDAI, RBI or the insurer's head office; fee, tax or charge demanded before the payout is released; repeated new charges after each payment; complaint or claim website that is not bimabharosa.irdai.gov.in or the insurer's site
investment_trading:
SCAM PATTERN: Investment or trading app (id investment_trading, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Victims are added to WhatsApp or Telegram 'stock tips' or IPO groups, shown fake profits on an app, and asked to keep depositing, then to pay 'tax' or 'fees' before they can withdraw.
Channels: whatsapp, telegram, social, app. Payment rails: neft_rtgs, imps, upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Retired professionals and bank officials appear in reported cases (e.g. a retired Mumbai scientist, a Palghar bank official); no official target profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: Our members made 300% this month.; Pay the 20% tax to release your profit.; join our VIP group for guaranteed daily profits; we will open an institutional account so you get IPO allotment; our firm is SEBI registered, here is the certificate; pay 10 percent tax to release your profit
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: Guaranteed or very high returns; Tips group on WhatsApp or Telegram; Must pay to withdraw profits; Payee is an individual, not a registered broker; added to a WhatsApp or Telegram group sharing 'VIP' stock tips; trading app downloaded from a link, not the Play Store or App Store
invoice_mandate_redirection:
SCAM PATTERN: Invoice / mandate redirection (payment diversion, BEC) (id invoice_mandate_redirection, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A criminal who has compromised or spoofed the email of a supplier, solicitor, conveyancer, builder or title company tells the payer that bank details have changed, or sends a genuine-looking invoice with new payee details, so a payment the victim intended for a legitimate payee goes to the criminal's account. It hits both businesses (supplier invoices) and consumers (house deposits, tradespeople).
Channels: email, call. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire.
Typical victims: Businesses and their finance staff, and consumers paying solicitors, conveyancers or tradespeople; UK Finance: 68% of 2025 invoice and mandate losses were on non-personal (business) accounts. IC3 cases include home buyers closing on property.
What the fraudster typically claims: please note our bank details have changed, use the account below; here are the wire instructions for your closing; completion funds must reach us today; attached is the updated invoice
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: email saying supplier or solicitor bank details have changed; invoice with new payee account just before a large payment; sender address slightly different from the usual one; urgency to pay a house deposit or completion funds today; payee name on the new account does not match the business; first payment ever to this account for a known supplier
job_task_scam_global:
SCAM PATTERN: Task-based job scam (pay to unlock commissions) (id job_task_scam_global, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): An unsolicited text or WhatsApp/Telegram message, or a social media ad, offers easy remote work such as liking videos, rating products, apps or restaurants, or 'boosting' orders for a commission. After small early payouts, the victim is told to deposit their own money (often crypto or transfers to individuals) to unlock the next set of tasks, complete 'double tasks' or withdraw earnings, with group chats of fake members pushing them on; deposits grow until the victim cannot withdraw anything.
Channels: sms, whatsapp, telegram, social, app. Payment rails: crypto, bank_transfer, wallet.
Typical victims: SPF 1H 2026: job scam victims mostly aged 30-49 (38.6%), contacted mainly on WhatsApp and Facebook.
What the fraudster typically claims: earn money from home by liking videos or rating products; complete a set of 40 tasks to get your commission; you've got a double task with a bigger commission, top up to complete it; deposit more to withdraw your earnings; our team members earned thousands this week
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: recent unsolicited job offer by text or WhatsApp; payments to individuals or crypto exchange described as 'top-ups' for tasks; customer mentions commissions for liking, rating or reviewing; escalating deposits after small payouts; told to pay to withdraw earnings; no interview or contract
kyc_block:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake KYC update / account block (id kyc_block, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Messages or calls say the bank account, card, PAN or KYC will be blocked today unless the customer updates details through a link, an app or a payment, or shares an OTP.
Channels: sms, whatsapp, call, app, web, email. Payment rails: upi, imps, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: General public; RBI aims its warnings especially at those new to digital banking (BE(A)WARE preface). No specific profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: Your KYC has expired; your account will be blocked in 24 hours.; Update your PAN now through this link.; your SBI YONO account is closed today; update your PAN now; your account will be blocked as your KYC has expired; install this KYC app to avoid losing services; your Aadhaar details are incomplete; update immediately
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: 'Your account will be blocked today' by SMS, WhatsApp or call; A link or app to 'update KYC'; Request for OTP, PIN or a small payment; message says account/YONO/card will be blocked or closed today; link or APK file sent to 'update KYC', PAN or Aadhaar; sender is a mobile number rather than an official short code
loan_app_harassment:
SCAM PATTERN: Illegal instant loan app with extortion and recovery harassment (id loan_app_harassment, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Unauthorised instant loan apps, often installed via APK links outside the Play Store or disguised as finance tools, demand access to contacts, call logs, SMS, photos and location, then extort money through threats and harassment, including blackmail using data taken from the phone, with callers posing as company or recovery representatives. Police have linked such app networks to shell companies run for foreign operatives.
Channels: app, call, whatsapp, sms. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented in sources reviewed.
What the fraudster typically claims: pay today or we will message everyone in your contacts; your photos will be sent to your family and friends; you have defaulted, pay the penalty immediately
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: loan app installed from a link or APK, not from a known bank or NBFC; app demanded access to contacts, photos, SMS and location; threatening calls or messages to you or your contacts; callers posing as the company or recovery agents demand immediate payment; payment demanded to a personal UPI ID or a new account each time
loan_processing_fee:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake loan approval with upfront fee (id loan_processing_fee, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters advertise easy loans through fake websites, apps, calls or social media, sometimes using the name of a known lender or payment app, and tell the applicant the loan is approved. Before disbursal they demand upfront payments described as processing, insurance, GST or other charges, keep inventing new fees, and the loan never arrives.
Channels: call, web, app, whatsapp, social, sms. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer, wallet, cash.
Typical victims: Small borrowers seeking quick credit (e.g. a fruit vendor applying for a Rs 3 lakh loan, Indore police case 2026); otherwise general public.
What the fraudster typically claims: your loan is sanctioned, pay the processing fee to release it; insurance charge is mandatory before disbursal; pay GST on the loan amount first; one last charge and the money will be credited today; your loan is approved, no credit check needed; pay the insurance fee first and the loan will be released
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: loan approved without proper documents or credit check; asked to pay before receiving the loan; fees described as processing, insurance, GST, file charge or verification; lender uses a well-known brand name but contacts you on WhatsApp or a personal number; payment goes to a personal UPI ID or account; caller asks to take your phone or install an app to 'process' the loan
lpg_gas_connection:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake gas agency / LPG KYC / PNG disconnection / dealership (id lpg_gas_connection, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Messages in the name of LPG companies or city-gas utilities say an LPG booking needs renewal or KYC update to keep cylinder deliveries, or that piped gas will be cut tonight at 9:30 pm unless the bill is updated. Victims are asked to call a number, pay a small 'system update' fee and install an APK such as 'Gas Bill Update.apk' or 'BILL_UPDATE.apk', which captures banking credentials; a separate variant sends forged LPG distributorship/dealership letters demanding fees.
Channels: whatsapp, sms, call, app, web. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Household gas consumers; documented Mahanagar Gas victims include a 75-year-old retiree (Moneylife, Jun 2026); dealership variant targets would-be distributors.
What the fraudster typically claims: your gas connection will be disconnected tonight at 9:30 pm; your previous bill is not updated; call this number; update your LPG KYC to continue cylinder delivery; pay Rs 10 to update the system; your payment did not reflect; install this app to complete it; you have been selected for an LPG distributorship
What victims are coached to say or do: stay on the call while installing the 'bill update' app and entering bank details (victim kept on phone for 45 minutes in one Mumbai case)
Red flags: WhatsApp message with gas company logo from a personal number; threat that gas supply will be cut tonight (e.g. 9:30 pm); LPG booking 'renewal' or KYC update needed via link; request for a Rs 10 'system update' fee, then 'payment not received'; APK file named like a bill or gas update; dealership offer letter asking for registration or security fees
matrimonial_fraud:
SCAM PATTERN: Matrimonial-site fraud (fake NRI / doctor / army groom or bride) (id matrimonial_fraud, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters create attractive fake profiles on matrimonial sites and apps, posing as NRIs, doctors, engineers, army officers or rich businesspeople, and quickly build an emotional bond and talk of marriage. Once trusted they ask for money on pretexts such as customs duty on a gift or on currency they were 'caught' with at the airport (often voiced by a fake airport/customs official), travel or visa costs, medical emergencies, or 'investment', and keep inventing new fees until the victim stops.
Channels: web, app, whatsapp, call. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer, crypto.
Typical victims: Prospective brides and grooms on matrimonial platforms; I4C notes fraudsters screen targets by age, income and profession. Reported cases involve women professionals.
What the fraudster typically claims: I have sent you expensive gifts and cash, just pay the customs charges; I am detained at Mumbai airport with foreign currency, pay the clearance fee; I need money for my visa and ticket to come to India; if you love me, please help me now; I trust only you; invest with me on this crypto platform for our future
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: match claims to live abroad or be a doctor/army officer and avoids video calls or meeting; marriage proposed very quickly; money requested for customs, gift clearance, visa, ticket or emergency; a third party 'airport/customs official' calls asking for fees; payment to a personal account unrelated to customs
mobile_tower_installation:
SCAM PATTERN: Mobile tower installation / lease fee scam (id mobile_tower_installation, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters promise property owners high monthly rent and a lump-sum advance for installing a mobile tower on their land or rooftop, then demand upfront payments described as government tax under the Telecom Act, registration, NOC or security fees, backed by forged TRAI/DoT letters and fake No Objection Certificates. After collecting money they become unreachable.
Channels: call, sms, web, social, email, whatsapp. Payment rails: bank_transfer, imps, neft_rtgs, upi.
Typical victims: Owners of land, rooftops or premises seeking rental income; no further profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: your property is approved for a mobile tower with high monthly rent; pay the government tax under the Telecom Act to proceed; here is your NOC from TRAI/DoT; pay the processing fee; you will receive a large advance once the security deposit is paid
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: unsolicited offer of high rent for installing a mobile tower; upfront 'government tax', registration, NOC or security fee; letter or NOC claiming to be from TRAI, DoT or the Ministry of Communications; payment to a personal or private company account; pressure to pay quickly to 'book' the site
mule_account_recruitment:
SCAM PATTERN: Renting or selling your bank account or SIM (money mule) (id mule_account_recruitment, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraud networks pay people a commission or fee to hand over or 'rent' their bank accounts, debit cards, net-banking access or SIM cards, or to receive money and forward it. These mule accounts and SIMs are then used to receive and launder proceeds of investment, task, APK and other frauds; account holders who sell or rent them face arrest, and police have also arrested bank employees who helped open such accounts.
Channels: whatsapp, telegram, social, in_person, call, sms, app. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer, card, cash, wallet, crypto.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented in sources reviewed (cases include account holders and bank staff).
What the fraudster typically claims: sell or lend your account and earn a commission on every amount that passes through; money will come in, forward it to this account and keep your share; the job is just transferring money and receiving packages for us; you'll be paid for moving funds through your account; let us use your bank account or Singpass for a while; send the money on to this account and keep something for yourself
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: offer of commission or monthly rent for using your bank account; asked to hand over debit card, passbook, cheque book, net-banking login or SIM; asked to open a new account or SIM in your name for someone else; money arrives from strangers and you are told to forward it; told to withdraw cash or send money onward and keep a percentage; incoming payments from unknown people followed quickly by outgoing transfers
pension_life_certificate:
SCAM PATTERN: Pensioner life certificate / pension office impersonation (id pension_life_certificate, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): During the annual life-certificate season, callers posing as the pension department or CPAO contact pensioners, quote their PPO number, retirement date, Aadhaar and nominee details to sound genuine, and say the life certificate must be updated online or the pension will be affected. They ask for an OTP or personal details 'to update the certificate' and then take over and drain the pension account.
Channels: call, sms, whatsapp. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Senior-citizen pensioners, especially elderly or unwell people who find it hard to visit a bank branch (Moneylife 2022; CPAO notice).
What the fraudster typically claims: I am calling from the pension department about your life certificate; your life certificate is not updated; your pension will stop; tell me the OTP to update your life certificate online; we have your PPO number; just confirm your details
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: call claiming to be from the pension office, treasury or CPAO; caller already knows PPO number, retirement date or Aadhaar; says the life certificate must be updated by phone or online now; asks for an OTP, bank details or personal information; warns the pension will stop if you do not act
pig_butchering_crypto:
SCAM PATTERN: Pig butchering / fake crypto or trading platform investment (id pig_butchering_crypto, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): Scammers make contact through a wrong-number text, dating app, social media ad or 'investment learning' WhatsApp/Telegram group with fake mentors and members, build trust, then direct the victim to a fake crypto or trading app that shows growing profits. Victims deposit progressively larger sums (bank transfer to 'agents', crypto, or even cash handed to couriers) and when they try to withdraw are hit with 'taxes' or 'fees' before the scammers disappear. Many operations run from Southeast Asian scam compounds using trafficked workers.
Channels: sms, social, whatsapp, telegram, app, web. Payment rails: bank_transfer, crypto, card, cash, wire.
