Typical victims: general public; IC3 2025 reports crypto investment fraud complainants aged 60+ (13,685 complaints) lost $2.76 billion, the most of any age group; SPF says investment victims are reached via online acquaintances, ads, searches and chat groups.
What the fraudster typically claims: join our free investment learning community; our mentor's stock picks made 30% this week; you need to deposit more to reach VIP level; pay the withdrawal tax first and your profits will be released; I made a fortune trading crypto, let me teach you
What victims are coached to say or do: tell the bank the money is for home renovation; the bank will try to stop you, give them a different reason; use the cover story if the branch asks why you are withdrawing cash
Red flags: first-time transfers to a crypto exchange or to individuals described as 'agents'; customer mentions a mentor, trading group or app showing big profits; escalating deposits after small early withdrawals; request to pay 'tax' or 'fees' before withdrawing profits; contact began with a wrong-number text, dating match or social ad; large cash withdrawal said to be for an investment
ponzi_deposit_scheme:
SCAM PATTERN: Ponzi / unregulated deposit, chit or MLM scheme (id ponzi_deposit_scheme, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A company, 'chit fund' or network scheme collects deposits from the public through commission agents, relatives or community members, promising unusually high fixed returns or bonuses for recruiting others. Early investors are paid from later deposits until the scheme stops paying and collapses; such schemes are unregistered with any financial regulator, which is itself an offence under the BUDS Act, 2019.
Channels: in_person, whatsapp, social, call. Payment rails: cash, upi, bank_transfer, neft_rtgs.
Typical victims: Small depositors reached through local commission agents (Saradha case); no specific profile documented in official sources reviewed.
What the fraudster typically claims: your money will double in a short time; guaranteed monthly return, better than any bank; bring two more members and earn extra commission; this is a registered chit fund, completely safe
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: fixed returns far above bank deposit rates; money collected by agents who earn commission; bonus or higher return for bringing in new members; scheme is not registered with RBI, SEBI or another regulator; pressure to reinvest rather than withdraw; delays in paying returns explained as temporary
prize_lottery:
SCAM PATTERN: Prize, lottery or gift fee (id prize_lottery, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): The victim is told they have won a lottery, a quiz prize or a gift from abroad, and must pay processing fees, taxes or customs duty before it can be released.
Channels: whatsapp, call, sms, email, web. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented (cases include homemakers and young adults).
What the fraudster typically claims: You won 25 lakh in the KBC lucky draw; pay the GST first.; Your foreign gift is held at customs.; congratulations, your number has won Rs 25 lakh in the KBC Jio lottery; call our lottery manager on WhatsApp to claim; pay the refundable processing fee and GST first; your prize has increased to Rs 45 lakh, pay the extra tax
What victims are coached to say or do: contact the manager only on WhatsApp; keep the prize secret until it is credited; pay the processing fee and GST first; it is refundable
Red flags: A prize from a contest never entered; Fee or tax before payout; Gift stuck at customs; you 'won' a lottery or draw you never entered; message from a foreign (+92) number using KBC, Jio or celebrity images; fee, GST or tax must be paid before the prize is released
purchase_scam_marketplace:
SCAM PATTERN: Purchase scam (fake seller: goods, vehicles, pets, tickets, holiday lets) (id purchase_scam_marketplace, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A fake seller on a marketplace, social media or a cloned website advertises an item or service below market price (phones, cars, pets, concert tickets, collectibles, holiday rentals) and persuades the buyer to pay by bank transfer or cash rather than the platform's protected payment, sometimes as a 'deposit' or pre-order with delivery promised weeks or months later. After payment the seller disappears; the reverse variant targets sellers with fake proof-of-payment screenshots.
Channels: marketplace, social, web, whatsapp, telegram. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wallet, cash, wire.
Typical victims: Broad and mostly lower-value: UK Finance says 71% of 2025 APP cases were purchase scams with an average loss of £671; SPF says e-commerce victims were mostly aged 30-49 (41.3%) and contacted on Carousell and Telegram.
What the fraudster typically claims: lots of people want it, pay a deposit now to secure it; pay by bank transfer, the platform's payment doesn't work for me; I'll courier it to you as soon as payment clears; pre-order now, delivery in a few months; I've already sent payment, here's the screenshot
What victims are coached to say or do: pay by bank transfer instead of the platform's secure payment option; pay in cash or by money transfer service
Red flags: payment by bank transfer to an individual for an item found on a marketplace or social media; price well below market value; seller insists on paying off-platform or refuses card/escrow; deposit or pre-order for a car, pet, tickets or holiday let not yet seen; payee name differs from the seller's name; urgency because 'other buyers are interested'
qr_code_receive:
SCAM PATTERN: Scan QR code to 'receive' payment (id qr_code_receive, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A fake buyer, frequently claiming to be an Army or paramilitary officer posted far away, agrees to buy something listed online, sends a fake payment screenshot and then a QR code, and guides the seller to scan it and enter the UPI PIN to 'receive' the money. Each scan debits the seller; the fraudster then sends a QR for double the amount to 'reverse the mistake', repeating until the victim stops.
Channels: marketplace, whatsapp, call. Payment rails: upi.
Typical victims: Sellers advertising goods on online classified sites such as OLX and Quikr (Delhi Police).
What the fraudster typically claims: I am in the Army, posted far away, so I will pay online; scan this QR code and the payment will come to you; there was a technical issue, scan this one to get your money back; I sent double by mistake, scan again to fix it
What victims are coached to say or do: scan this QR code and enter your UPI PIN to receive the payment; scan the new QR code to get your money refunded
Red flags: buyer agrees to the price instantly without seeing the item; buyer claims to be in the Army or posted at a remote location and sends an ID card; buyer sends a QR code and asks you to scan it to receive payment; app asks for UPI PIN after scanning the buyer's code; after money is lost, buyer sends a new QR for a bigger amount to 'refund' it; fake payment screenshot instead of a real credit in the account
rbi_fictitious_funds:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake RBI official: release of lottery / foreign funds / bonus after fees (id rbi_fictitious_funds, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Letters, emails, SMS or calls using RBI-like letterheads, fake websites or the names of real RBI officials tell victims that lottery winnings, funds from abroad or other payouts are waiting, and ask for small 'processing', tax-clearance, conversion or clearing fees into specified bank accounts, followed by ever larger demands. Impostors posing as RBI officials have also used insurance-bonus stories to extract large sums.
Channels: call, email, sms, web, whatsapp. Payment rails: bank_transfer, neft_rtgs, imps, upi.
Typical victims: General public; documented victims include an 82-year-old retired professor (Moneylife 2022).
What the fraudster typically claims: RBI has approved release of your foreign remittance; pay the conversion charges; you have won a lottery; RBI will release the funds after tax clearance; I am a deputy general manager at RBI handling your payout; deposit the processing fee in this account to receive your funds
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: message or call claiming RBI holds money or a payout for you; letter signed in the name of an RBI official with a contact number; fees for processing, tax clearance or currency conversion before release; payments to accounts of individuals or proprietary firms; fake website resembling RBI's
recovery_room_scam:
SCAM PATTERN: Recovery room / fund recovery scam (id recovery_room_scam, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): People who have already lost money (often to investment or crypto scams) are contacted by, or find online ads for, fake law firms, 'asset recovery' companies, government agencies or police who say they can trace and recover the lost funds. Victims are asked for an upfront fee, a percentage, a 'tax', personal and bank details, or remote access, and then for more payments to continue the 'investigation'; nothing is recovered.
Channels: call, email, social, web, sms, whatsapp. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, crypto, card, upi, gift_card, wallet.
Typical victims: Previous scam victims, whose details are traded on 'sucker lists' (FTC). IC3 2025: 60+ complainants reported $540.5m of recovery-scam losses, the most of any age group.
What the fraudster typically claims: we have traced your stolen crypto and can return it; we are a law firm working with the authorities on your case; pay the release fee and your funds will be returned within days; your refund is ready, we just need your bank details; the investigation needs another payment to continue; we have traced and frozen your lost money
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: customer was recently scammed and is now paying a 'recovery' firm or lawyer; fee, percentage or tax demanded before funds are returned; caller claims to be police, a regulator or a government body offering to recover money; request for remote access or bank details to 'deposit' a refund; repeat payments to fund an 'investigation'; recovery service found via online ad promising to trace crypto
refund_cashback:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake refund / cashback payout (id refund_cashback, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A victim waiting for a refund (failed payment, cancelled order, overcharge) or lured by a 'cashback' or reward is contacted by, or calls, a fake customer care agent often found through a search engine. The agent tells them to scan a QR code, approve a request, enter their UPI PIN, pay a small 'verification' amount or install an app 'to process the refund', which instead sends money out or hands over the account.
Channels: call, web, whatsapp, sms, app. Payment rails: upi, card, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Customers seeking refunds from food delivery, airline and travel platforms who searched online for helpline numbers (Hyderabad police cases, 2020); otherwise general public.
What the fraudster typically claims: your refund is approved, scan this to receive it; enter your UPI PIN to get the refund credited; pay Rs 10 to verify your account and the refund will come; you have won cashback, approve the request to claim it
What victims are coached to say or do: scan this code and enter your PIN to get your refund; approve the pending request to release your refund or cashback; install this app so we can process your refund
Red flags: customer care number found through a Google or Justdial search rather than the official app; agent asks for UPI PIN, OTP or card details to issue a refund; refund requires scanning a QR code or approving a payment request; asked to pay a small token amount (e.g. Rs 5-100) to 'verify' the account; asked to install a remote-access or support app
relative_emergency:
SCAM PATTERN: Relative in trouble (id relative_emergency, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller (sometimes with a cloned or crying voice) says a son, daughter or relative has been arrested or hurt and needs money immediately, and asks the victim not to tell anyone.
Channels: call, whatsapp. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Parents and elderly relatives of students or of children living in other cities or abroad (e.g. Canada, US), per police and news reports.
What the fraudster typically claims: Your son has been caught; pay now and we will let him go.; Don't call anyone, it will make it worse.; your son has been arrested in a rape case; your daughter is in police custody with drugs; your son in Canada has caused an accident and someone is in a coma; pay now and we will settle the matter with senior officers
What victims are coached to say or do: do not hang up the call; do not contact your son; his phone is with the police; do not tell anyone or report it, just pay to settle the matter
Red flags: Urgent call about a relative; Victim has not spoken to the relative; Payment to a stranger's account; Told to keep it quiet; call from an unknown, foreign or WhatsApp number claiming the child is in custody or in an accident; crying or distressed voice played as proof
remote_access:
SCAM PATTERN: Screen-sharing takeover (id remote_access, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): The caller gets the victim to install a remote-access app or an unknown APK, then watches or controls the phone while the victim 'verifies' a payment.
Channels: call, web, sms, app. Payment rails: upi, imps, card, bank_transfer, wallet.
Typical victims: general public; customers seeking help for a refund, KYC, blocked account or failed transaction (RBI, Hyderabad police); no narrower profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: Install this app so our technician can fix it.; Share your screen while you complete verification.; install this app so I can fix your problem; tell me the code shown on your screen; open your banking app so I can process the refund
What victims are coached to say or do: install this support app and share the code on your screen; keep the app open and log in to your bank app while I guide you
Red flags: Asked to install an app or APK; Asked to share screen; Someone guiding taps during the payment; agent asks you to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer, QuickSupport or another 'support' app; asked to read out a 9-digit or similar access code; asked to open your bank or UPI app while the call or screen share is on
rent_advance_landlord:
SCAM PATTERN: Rental fraud by fake army / NSG tenant (send money to receive the rent advance) (id rent_advance_landlord, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): After an owner lists a flat on a real-estate portal or social media, a caller posing as an Army, NSG or CRPF officer 'being transferred' agrees to rent it without visiting and sends a uniformed photo and forged ID. A 'senior officer' or 'Army accountant' then says defence payment rules require a 'reversal mode' or a payment to 'raise a demand', gets the owner to send a small test amount (sometimes returned to build trust), then the advance and ever larger sums, or to click payment links, promising everything will be refunded with the rent. Police also report fake rental listings that take advances from would-be tenants, but the documented army-officer cases mostly target owners.
Channels: call, whatsapp, web, marketplace. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Property owners advertising flats for rent on housing portals and social media, per Hyderabad and Andaman & Nicobar police.
What the fraudster typically claims: I am an army officer transferred here, I will take the flat without visiting; our accountant will pay the advance through army reversal mode; send Rs 5 first to test, it will come back; due to defence security protocol you must pay to raise the demand; the system failed, send again and everything will be refunded
What victims are coached to say or do: send a small test amount first; it will be credited back; pay the amount to 'raise a demand' so the army system releases the advance; keep transferring until the system acknowledges and refunds everything; enter the advance amount yourself in the payment link
Red flags: prospective tenant claims to be army/NSG/CRPF and recently transferred; agrees to rent without seeing the property; a 'senior officer' or 'army accountant' handles the payment; owner asked to pay first, send a test amount, or type the advance amount into a link; 'system failure' leads to repeated transfers with promised refunds; uniformed DP, patriotic slogans, forged service ID
romance_scam_global:
SCAM PATTERN: Romance scam (online partner asks for money) (id romance_scam_global, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A fraudster with a fake profile on a dating site or social media builds an intense online relationship over weeks or months, avoids video calls and meetings, then asks for money for a crisis (visa, medical bills, flight tickets, stuck customs package, business or oil-rig problems) or steers the victim into a fake investment. Requests repeat and grow, and victims are often asked to keep the relationship secret and become isolated from family.
Channels: social, web, app, whatsapp, telegram. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, gift_card, crypto, wallet.
Typical victims: general public; Report Fraud notes victims are isolated from family and friends and for almost a third the fraud lasts over a year; no age profile stated in the sources opened
What the fraudster typically claims: I'm stuck abroad and need money for the visa; my package is held at customs, can you pay the fee; I'm on an oil rig and can't access my accounts; I'll pay you back as soon as I get home; let me show you how I invest in crypto
What victims are coached to say or do: don't tell anyone about us; keep this between us, your family won't understand
Red flags: repeated payments to a person the customer has never met; payee abroad or a third party 'agent'; story of visa, medical, customs or travel costs; relationship began online and moved to WhatsApp/Telegram; customer reluctant to discuss the payee or told to keep it secret; escalating amounts over weeks or months
romance_social_media:
SCAM PATTERN: Romance / friendship scam via dating apps and social media (id romance_social_media, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters use fake or stolen-photo profiles on dating apps (Tinder, Bumble), Instagram and Facebook, posing as doctors, businesspeople, NRIs or defence personnel, and spend weeks or months building an emotional relationship. They then ask for money for sudden medical emergencies, business losses or family problems, or steer the victim into a fake 'investment'; a related in-person variant lures dating-app matches to a cafe or pub where the victim is coerced into paying a hugely inflated bill.
Channels: social, app, whatsapp, call, in_person. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer, card, crypto.
Typical victims: Users of dating apps, Instagram and matrimonial sites; I4C notes targets are filtered by age and income. Reported cases include women targeted by a serial conman and men lured by female profiles.
What the fraudster typically claims: my mother is in hospital, I need money urgently; my business account is frozen, I will return it next week; I love you and trust only you; let us invest together for our future; it is my birthday, meet me at this cafe
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: online-only partner never met in person asks for money; sudden emergency (hospital, business loss, family crisis) right after trust is built; refuses live video call or keeps changing identity; pushes a crypto or trading 'investment' together; first date at a venue chosen by the match followed by an enormous bill
scholarship_fee:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake scholarship sanction / processing fee (id scholarship_fee, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Pattern as scoped for Ruko: students or parents are told by call, SMS or WhatsApp that a government scholarship or student benefit has been sanctioned and must be 'released' after paying a processing/registration fee or sharing bank details and OTPs. Evidence status: no source fetched in this run documented this exact script; documented neighbours are PIB-flagged student-benefit hoaxes such as a fake 'Students' Laptop Scheme 2025' phishing link, and the general rule that genuine schemes never charge registration or processing fees.
Channels: call, sms, whatsapp, web, social. Payment rails: upi, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Students and their parents (inferred from the scheme type; no source in this run profiles victims).
What the fraudster typically claims: your scholarship has been approved; pay the processing fee to receive it; register on this link for the student scheme; share the OTP to link your bank account for the scholarship amount
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: unsolicited message saying a scholarship is sanctioned; fee demanded to release or process the scholarship; link that is not scholarships.gov.in or a state .gov.in portal; request for bank details, Aadhaar or OTP by phone; deadline pressure to pay today
sim_disconnection:
SCAM PATTERN: SIM or number disconnection (id sim_disconnection, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A recorded or live call claiming to be from TRAI or the telecom department says the victim's number will be disconnected for illegal activity, then hands them to fake police.
Channels: call, whatsapp, video, sms. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: General public; documented victims include retirees (e.g. a retired Air Force employee in Faridabad, PTI via Deccan Herald, Nov 2024).
What the fraudster typically claims: Your number will be blocked in two hours. Press 9 to speak to an officer.; your mobile number will be disconnected within two hours; another SIM in your name is being used for illegal activities; a complaint/FIR is registered against your number; you need a police clarification letter to keep your number; I am transferring you to the cyber crime police
What victims are coached to say or do: do not disconnect the call or action will be taken against your family (reported in the Faridabad digital-arrest case that began with a fake TRAI call)
Red flags: Call 'from TRAI' or 'DoT'; Number to be cut off within hours; Transferred to police; IVR call saying your number will be blocked in two hours; asked to press 9 to speak to a TRAI or DoT officer; claim that a SIM issued on your Aadhaar was used for crime or harassment
sim_swap_esim:
SCAM PATTERN: SIM swap / eSIM activation / '5G SIM upgrade' (id sim_swap_esim, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters posing as telecom operator staff call or text about a SIM upgrade, 5G upgrade, KYC or eSIM activation and get the victim to click a link, share an OTP or confirm a code. The victim's number moves to a SIM or eSIM controlled by the fraudster, the victim's phone loses signal, and bank OTPs and alerts go to the fraudster, who resets credentials and drains accounts.
Channels: call, sms, email. Payment rails: upi, imps, neft_rtgs, bank_transfer, card.
Typical victims: I4C says users of all age groups are targeted (as reported by Digit, 2025); no narrower profile documented.
What the fraudster typically claims: your SIM will be blocked today unless you upgrade; we will upgrade your SIM to 5G free, just share the OTP; click this link to activate your eSIM; your KYC for the SIM is pending
What victims are coached to say or do: click the link to activate your eSIM; share the OTP to complete the 5G upgrade
Red flags: call or SMS offering a free 4G-to-5G SIM upgrade or eSIM activation; link or code to 'activate eSIM' that you did not request; phone suddenly shows no signal or 'SIM not registered'; OTPs and bank SMS stop arriving; caller claims to be from Jio, Airtel, Vi or BSNL and asks for an OTP
task_job:
SCAM PATTERN: Part-time job or task (id task_job, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Offers of easy work (liking videos, rating hotels, reviews) pay small amounts at first, then require 'prepaid tasks' or deposits to unlock larger earnings that are never paid.
Channels: whatsapp, telegram, social, web. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer, crypto.
Typical victims: Retired employees, women and unemployed youth looking for part-time work (MHA/I4C as reported by The News Minute, 2023).
What the fraudster typically claims: Complete 3 prepaid tasks to withdraw your commission.; Your account is frozen until you pay the reset fee.; earn from home just by liking YouTube videos; rate restaurants and get commission daily; this is a prepaid task, deposit to get higher returns; you made a mistake in the task, pay to repair it
What victims are coached to say or do: pay the task repair amount to unlock your withdrawal; your credit score is low, pay this to release the money
Red flags: Paid to like, review or rate; Small payouts first; Must deposit to unlock earnings; unsolicited offer of Rs 500-1,000+ a day for liking videos or giving reviews; moved from WhatsApp to a Telegram 'VIP' or 'task' group; small first payouts, then a request to deposit money to unlock bigger tasks
tech_support_refund:
SCAM PATTERN: Tech support / refund-overpayment scam (remote access) (id tech_support_refund, region global)
How it works (from official advisories): A fake security pop-up, renewal notice (Geek Squad, McAfee, Norton), Amazon/Microsoft/bank message or cold call leads the victim to a fake technician or refund agent, who gets them to install remote access software (AnyDesk, UltraViewer, ConnectWise). The scammer then either moves money out while the victim is logged in to banking, or stages a fake 'refund', claims too much was paid and pressures the victim to send back the 'overpayment' by transfer, gift cards, crypto or cash. The story often escalates to a fake bank or government agent telling the victim to move savings to 'protect' them.
Channels: web, call, email, sms. Payment rails: bank_transfer, wire, gift_card, crypto, cash, card.
Typical victims: Older adults are prominent: FTC (2025) reports older adults losing $10,000+ to these impersonators quadrupled 2020-2024; IC3 2025 lists tech support/ATO as the top crime type in elder-fraud recovery incidents.
What the fraudster typically claims: your computer has been hacked, call this number now; your subscription will auto-renew for hundreds of dollars unless you cancel; we refunded you too much by mistake, please send the difference back; install this app so we can fix the firewall; your bank account is compromised, we will transfer you to the fraud team
What victims are coached to say or do: stay on the phone and do not talk to anyone else; log into your bank so we can process the refund; approve the transaction on your token or app when it pops up
Red flags: pop-up or message telling the customer to call a support number; remote access app installed during a call; customer logs into banking while a 'technician' is connected; claim that a refund was overpaid and must be sent back; request to pay a company or 'refund' via gift cards, crypto or Bitcoin ATM; hand-off from tech support to a 'bank' or 'government' agent
travel_pilgrimage_booking:
SCAM PATTERN: Fake pilgrimage / travel booking (Kedarnath helicopter, Char Dham, hotels, cabs) (id travel_pilgrimage_booking, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): Fraudsters run fake websites, social-media pages, WhatsApp accounts and even paid Google/Facebook ads offering Kedarnath helicopter tickets, Char Dham yatra packages, guest-house and hotel rooms, cabs and religious tour packages, often misusing names of real booking platforms. Pilgrims and tourists pay by UPI or transfer to confirm, receive fake tickets or nothing, and the contact goes silent.
Channels: web, social, whatsapp, call. Payment rails: upi, bank_transfer, card.
Typical victims: Religious pilgrims and tourists, per the I4C alert.
What the fraudster typically claims: Kedarnath helicopter tickets available, confirm now with advance; guaranteed Char Dham package, limited seats; pay the full amount by UPI and we will send the ticket on WhatsApp; hotel near the temple, pay 50% advance to block the room; official booking agent, IRCTC quota
What victims are coached to say or do: (none documented)
Red flags: helicopter or darshan booking offered outside the official IRCTC/state portal; booking found via a sponsored search ad or social-media page; payment requested to a personal UPI ID or individual's account; very cheap or 'guaranteed' tickets during peak season; agent communicates only on WhatsApp and sends a ticket image
upi_collect_request:
SCAM PATTERN: UPI collect request ('enter PIN to receive money') (id upi_collect_request, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): The fraudster, often posing as a buyer, refund desk or cashback provider, sends a UPI 'collect' (request money) and tells the victim to approve it and enter the UPI PIN to receive money; approving actually debits the victim. NPCI's circular dated 29 July 2025 (as reported) stops person-to-person collect requests from 1 October 2025, but merchant collect requests continue, so payment requests that need a PIN still reach users.
Channels: call, whatsapp, sms, marketplace, app. Payment rails: upi.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented
What the fraudster typically claims: I have sent you a request, just approve it and the money will come to you; enter your UPI PIN to receive the refund; approve the request to claim your cashback; this is how our payment system sends money to sellers
What victims are coached to say or do: approve the request and enter your UPI PIN to receive the money
Red flags: a payment request appears in the UPI app while someone on the phone says you are receiving money; you are asked to enter your UPI PIN to get a refund, cashback, prize or buyer payment; the request screen shows 'pay' or a debit amount, not a credit; the requester is a stranger, a marketplace buyer or a 'customer care' caller; pressure to approve quickly before the request 'expires'
video_call_blackmail:
SCAM PATTERN: Video-call blackmail (id video_call_blackmail, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): After a video call with a stranger, the victim is threatened with an edited or recorded video and told to pay or it will be sent to family; fake 'police' may follow up.
Channels: video, whatsapp, social, call. Payment rails: upi, imps, bank_transfer.
Typical victims: Sources describe mostly men contacted through social media, dating apps or unknown WhatsApp video calls; police note both men and women can be targeted.
What the fraudster typically claims: Pay now or the video goes to all your contacts.; your video is recorded and will go viral if you do not pay; I am an inspector from the cyber crime cell; a case will be filed against you; the woman in the video attempted suicide and her family has evidence; I am from YouTube; pay and we will delete the uploaded video; you will lose your job if this comes out
What victims are coached to say or do: pay a fee so the video is deleted from YouTube; pay to have the police case settled or closed; keep paying in instalments to stop the video being released
Red flags: Threat to share a video or photos; Repeated demands after each payment; unknown or new contact initiates a WhatsApp video call that turns sexual; threat to send a recorded or morphed video to family or contacts; a 'police officer' or 'YouTube official' calls about the same video demanding money; repeated escalating demands after a first small payment
wrong_transfer_return:
SCAM PATTERN: 'Sent by mistake, please return' with fake credit SMS (id wrong_transfer_return, region india)
How it works (from official advisories): A caller posing as a relative's friend or acquaintance says he owes or is sending money to the family and will transfer it to the victim. While on the line he sends fake 'credited' SMSes from an ordinary mobile number, then claims he sent too much by mistake (e.g. 30,000 instead of 3,000) and urgently asks for the difference back, often citing a hospital emergency; no money ever arrived.
Channels: call, sms, whatsapp. Payment rails: upi, imps.
Typical victims: general public; no specific profile documented
What the fraudster typically claims: I am your father's friend, he asked me to send money to you; I sent 30,000 instead of 3,000 by mistake, please return the rest; check your SMS, the money has come; I am at the hospital, please send it back quickly
What victims are coached to say or do: return the extra money immediately, I am at the hospital; check your SMS inbox to verify the credit and send back the excess; send the return to this other UPI ID
Red flags: unknown caller claims to know your father or another relative; credit alert SMS comes from a 10-digit mobile number, not the bank's sender ID; caller says he sent extra by mistake and asks for the excess back; bank app balance does not show the credit; caller stays on the line, pushes urgency or a medical emergency; refund to be sent to a different UPI ID or number than the sender
